In this context, school district boundaries are likely to be more significant than the boundaries between general purpose local government units. Thus the "city or village" unit should be ignored in migration studies in many areas, and projection for cities and villages to emerge simply as totals of the projections for the districts which constitute the city or village.
As economic base and labor force considerations dominate the analysis of migration at the metro level, so housing availability and levels of residential services and amenities dominate migration studies at the district level.
Districts may be regarded as competing for population on the basis of their predominant type, density and quality of housing, levels of residential services such as schools, social prestige, safety, and amenity, and consideration of cost and accessibility to employment and region-serving facilities.
Though highly judgmental, this process is disciplined by the requirement that all of the migrants to one district must also appear as migrants from other districts, and vice versa. The United States adult population can be expected to move and past data shows that about one-fifth move in a given year and about one-half will stay in the same residence for at least five years.
The annual school-age population censuses conducted can be used to obtain relatively good information on migration flows among districts. As previously noted, the social considerations, which in most cases are a family judgement with each family placing more emphasis on different values, are related to migration between districts. Therefore, a "district" in a large metropolitan area would be defined as a "neighborhood".
In 1970, the Village of Matteson, Park Forest, Olympia Fields and the City of Chicago Heights did not differ substantially from the average suburb in Northeastern Illinois insofar as the data that is available indicates.
